catalog_quote: 2.1.6 LEVEL 6 - THE PHONOLOGICAL WORD. Phonological words contain syllables which are grouped together rhythmically and carry at least a third degree of stress. Phrase or clause stress may also occur on the same syllable obscurring the word stress. Words are of three types: type 1: single syllable -'biñ AB1, C1. type 2: two syllables with stress on the first syllable 'ani- AB1, C2; -'pulaŋ AB1, C5 type 3: three syllables with stress on the first syllable 'aṛiṭu- AB2, C4 [p. 19] On phonological words os [sic] type 2 or 3 the stress will shift to the second syllable if that syllable marks the beginning of a grammatical word. ... In this example, the final vowel a of wara 'he goes' is lost before the first vowel of the next word. The prefix an- always takes stress. So the resulting syllable ran is stressed. [p. 21, 2.2 Summary of Levels] Level 6: Word [syllables, third degree of stress] type 1 ['S] type 2 ['SS] or [S'S] (where grammatical word breaks occur after the first syllable) type ['SSS] or [S'SS] (where grammatical word breaks occur after the first syllable)

sweep_summary: Iwaidja (iwai1244) is not in the catalog. Both search-list titles are by Barbara Sayers. (1) Sayers & Pym 1977 'Notes on rhythmic patterning in Iwaidja' was found as an open PDF on the AuSIL publications page (https://ausil.org.au/language-documentation/ ->), saved and scanned, and read in full: it is a discourse-rhythm study and explicitly says word stress could not be identified by pitch; it gives no placement rule (prosody-but-not-word-stress; no catalog record). (2) Sayers 1977 'Prosodies in some Aboriginal languages' (WPNGL 20:91-100, Iwaidja + Wik-Mungkan per Glottolog) has no open copy anywhere reachable (archive.org holds only bibliography entries; sil.org search is JS/403; HathiTrust and Google Books blocked) — print only, medium priority. The same AuSIL page also yielded the full PDF of Pym 1979 'An analysis of discourse phonology' (WP-A-2), the deciding source the earlier our earlier reading ladder flagged as unfetchable and the prior search had only as FTS snippets; its §2.1.6 (pp. 18-19) and p. 21 summary give the best first-hand Iwaidja word-stress statement: initial stress on the (max. 3-syllable) phonological word, shifting to the second syllable when that syllable begins a grammatical word, prefix an- always stressed, phrase/clause stress may override. The complete Pym & Larrimore 1979 phonemes paper was also downloaded (silent on stress). all discovery went through archive.org APIs, Glottolog, ERIC API, AuSIL and automated download.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the first syllable of the (phonological) word; where a phonological word of two or three syllables contains a grammatical-word boundary after its first syllable, stress moves to the second syllable, i.e. to the initial syllable of the grammatical word. Word stress is the lowest (third) degree in a hierarchy below phrase stress (second heaviest) and clause stress (heaviest), which can override it. Capell 1962 §1.7 (held by the project) independently states initial stress ('Stress is normally on the first syllable of a di- or trisyllabic word') and Shaw et al. 2020:584 restate initial primary stress for unprefixed nominals.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Pym 1979 (snippets seen) does not describe secondary word stress; it describes three degrees of stress at clause/phrase/word level. Capell 1962 §1.7: 'in four syllable words there is a secondary stress on the third syllable', with 'a trochaic rhythm built up based on initial stress' in longer words.
new_statements.exceptions: Pym 1979: stress shifts to the second syllable when it begins a grammatical word; 'The prefix an- always takes stress'; phrase or clause stress may obscure word stress; the study's stated aim was to find out 'why word stress appeared to vary'. Capell 1962: 'occasionally final stresses are found, as in /ga'ralg/, his body'. Evans 2009: in X-n-X total reduplicants either half may be more heavily stressed depending on higher-level prosody.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the 'phonological word' of a discourse-phonology hierarchy (levels: discourse > paragraph > sentence > clause > phrase/rhythm group > word > syllable), based on narrative and procedural texts recorded 1974, not citation forms; the greatest clause-level stress 'is normally in the verb'. Shaw et al. 2020's statement is restricted to unprefixed nominals (Iwaidja is a prefixing language).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Iwaidja proper (iwai1244; Capell 1962 calls it Jiwadja, Cobourg Peninsula). Shaw et al. 2020 and the Caudal/Mailhammer work are based on Croker Island (Minjilang) speakers, the surviving community; Pym's 1974 texts come from the same Croker Island community (speakers coded AB and RK). No dialect distinction is drawn in any stress statement.

new_statements.reading: Initial stress on the phonological word (max. three syllables: ['S], ['SS], ['SSS]), shifting to the second syllable when that syllable begins a grammatical word (i.e. when a phonological word straddles a grammatical-word boundary: [S'S], [S'SS]); the prefix an- is always stressed; phrase and clause stress (second-heaviest / heaviest) can sit on the same syllable and obscure word stress. Longer grammatical words are split into several rhythm groups, so the statement does not determine secondary-stress alternation in 4+-syllable grammatical words; Pym also states that syllable grouping matters more than stress placement, whose variation does not affect intelligibility. Agrees with Capell 1962 (initial primary, secondary on 3rd of 4) and Shaw et al. 2020 (initial for unprefixed nominals).

new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (Pym's 'third degree of stress') falls on the first syllable of the phonological word, which has at most three syllables (['S], ['SS], ['SSS]); it shifts to the second syllable when that syllable begins a grammatical word (i.e. when a phonological word straddles a grammatical-word boundary: [S'S], [S'SS], summary table p. 21); the prefix an- is always stressed. Heavier degrees (phrase = second heaviest, clause = heaviest, normally on the verb) can sit on the same syllable and obscure word stress. Pym's introduction (p. 11) adds that syllable grouping matters more than stress placement and that 'variations in stress placement did not affect intelligibility to nearly the same extent'. Longer grammatical words are split into several rhythm groups, so the paper gives no alternating-stress rule for 4+-syllable grammatical words.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not as word-level secondary stress: Pym's three degrees of stress are the levels of a prosodic hierarchy (clause > phrase > word). Grammatical words longer than three syllables are broken into two phonological phrases/rhythm groups (p. 18 examples ananalangadbagba 'she teaches them', a-wanina:n 'they were sitting'), each rhythm group carrying its own stress. No statement of alternating secondary stress. (Capell 1962, held by the project from the earlier reading but not in this works list, gives secondary stress on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words.)
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shifts to the 2nd syllable of a type-2/3 phonological word when that syllable starts a grammatical word; the prefix an- always takes stress (so after vowel elision wara + angu- gives stressed ran); phrase/clause stress may override or obscure word stress; the author notes word stress 'appeared to vary' and that stress-placement variation barely affects intelligibility. The other five chapters of the volume (phonemes, verb system, phrases, narrative discourse, procedural discourse) mention stress only in the volume's symbol legend (° heaviest stress, " next heaviest stress, ' third degree of stress); intonation remarks there (clause-final falling intonation, list vs appositional intonation, 'Intonational features' p. 174) are not word-stress statements.
new_statements.identity_note: Pym's 1979 data are from Croker Island speakers recorded in 1972 and 1974 (texts AB, RK, EY); the volume introduction (p. v) locates Iwaidja on Croker Island, Coombe Point/Merganella and Snake Bay (Melville Island) = iwai1244. Bundgaard-Nielsen et al. 2025 treats Iwaidja (Croker Island) alongside Mawng (mawn1241); nothing dialect-specific about stress in either work.

sources.quote: These notes are the result of two weeks' field work at Croker Island in September 1974 to seek a solution to stress, length and pitch problems. The problems in previous analysis had been in identifying word stress. This problem was due to looking for the highest pitch as the contrastive feature of word stress. However, in normal conversation (responses) and in words elicited in isolation the syllables with highest pitch fluctuated from utterance to utterance of the same word. Also within a word two or more syllables frequently appeared to be equally stressed--that is, they had the same pitch and intensity.
